pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey near Welshpool in Powys, founded 1170 by Owain Cyfeiliog; it had the largest Cistercian church in Wales and almost nothing of it survives)
etymology: Latin strata Marcella, the Latin rendering of the Welsh Ystrad Marchell, the vale of Marchell.
biblical_def: Strata Marcella was founded in 1170 by Owain Cyfeiliog, prince of Powys, a daughter of Whitland, and its church was the largest the Cistercians ever raised in Wales. Owain himself took the habit there and died a monk. Today there is a field. Excavation in the nineteenth century found the foundations and a scatter of carved stone; the fabric went into farm buildings and the river took the rest. The abbey is therefore the strongest possible illustration of a verse that was written about men and applies without alteration to their works: “For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more” (Psa 103:16). The Psalmist is not being bleak. He sets that sentence beside the mercy that “is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him” (Psa 103:17), and the contrast is the point of the whole psalm. A prince who ended his days as a monk in the greatest church in Wales, and whose church is now pasture, has preached the first half; whether he believed the second half is between him and God, but the dictionary may say this much: the grass is the honest part. “As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psa 103:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ruin as the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or fortress; and perish as to die, to lose life in any manner, to be destroyed, to come to nothing.
webster_full: RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; defeat. The remains of a decayed or demolished city, house, fortress, or any work of men.
PERISH, v.i. To die; to lose life in any manner; to be destroyed; to come to nothing.
GRASS, n. In common usage, herbage; the plants which constitute the food of cattle and other beasts.
TRANSITORY, a. Passing without continuance; continuing a short time; fleeting; speedily vanishing.
VALE, n. A tract of low ground, or of land between hills; a valley.
scriptures: As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth.
For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more.
But the mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him, and his righteousness unto children's children;
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
corruption_summary: The greatest Cistercian church in Wales, founded by a prince who died in its habit, and now a field.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the confusion of permanence with significance — the builder's conviction that what endures in stone is what mattered. Owain Cyfeiliog was a poet as well as a prince and should have known better, and the order he joined had written the warning into its own statutes against ornament. The stones went to barns. What the psalm offers instead is not a smaller hope but a different one: “But the mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him” (Psa 103:17).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the word of God, and not the work of God's servants, is what abides. “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) is addressed to a people about to lose everything they had built, and it was enough for them. A congregation that loses a building has lost a building.
roots_summary: Latin strata, a paved way; Welsh ystrad, a vale; Hebrew chatsir (H2682), grass; Hebrew tsits (H6731), a flower; Hebrew chesed (H2617), covenant mercy.
roots_lines: Welsh ystrad — a vale or strath, Latinised as strata.
Hebrew chatsir (H2682) — grass, herbage; “his days are as grass” (Psa 103:15).
Hebrew tsits (H6731) — a blossom, a flower; “as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psa 103:15).
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — wind, breath; “For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone” (Psa 103:16).
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — steadfast covenant mercy; “from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him” (Psa 103:17).
usage: “the place thereof shall know it no more” (Psa 103:16) — said over a field near Welshpool.
“But the mercy of the LORD” (Psa 103:17) — the half that does not become pasture.
“but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) — the only masonry that holds.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Radnorshire, Wales, founded 1143; its nave was the longest in Wales and was never finished; burial place of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd)
etymology: Welsh cwm hir, the long valley — the abbey of the long valley, Latinised Abbatia de Cumbahir.
biblical_def: Abbeycwmhir was founded in 1143 and refounded in 1176 under the patronage of Cadwallon ap Madog. Its monks began a nave of fourteen bays, longer than any other in Wales and longer than most English cathedrals, and never finished it; the transepts and choir were never built to match. In December 1282 the headless body of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, the last native prince of Wales, was brought there for burial. The unfinished nave is the entry, because our Lord made exactly this an illustration: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?” (Luk 14:28), lest the onlookers say “This man began to build, and was not able to finish” (Luk 14:30). The parable is not about architecture or prudence in business. It stands in a passage about discipleship, and its force is that a half-built profession is worse than none, because it advertises in stone what the builder could not sustain. Cwmhir advertised it for four centuries. The valley kept the body of a prince and the footings of a church that was always too large for the house that owned it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines finish as to arrive at the end of, to bring to an end, to complete; and cost as the price, value or equivalent of a thing purchased, expense.
webster_full: FINISH, v.t. To arrive at the end of, in performance; to complete; as, to finish a house.
COST, n. The price, value or equivalent of a thing purchased; amount in value paid, charged or engaged to be paid for any thing bought or taken in barter.
NAVE, n. The middle or body of a church, extending from the balluster or rail of the door, to the chief choir.
PRESUMPTION, n. Blind or headstrong confidence; unreasonable adventurousness; a venturing to undertake something without sufficient warrant.
VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
scriptures: For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him,
Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.
So likewise, whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple.
corruption_summary: The longest nave in Wales, never finished, over the grave of the last native prince.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the overbuilt beginning — the project, the profession, the ministry launched at a scale its owner cannot carry, because the launching is what was enjoyed. Christ puts the mockery in the mouths of the onlookers and does not correct them: “all that behold it begin to mock him” (Luk 14:29) is reported as deserved. A church that starts what it cannot finish teaches the watching town that Christianity is a thing people start.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that counting the cost is a commanded act of discipleship, not caution opposed to faith. The parable ends where it was always going: “whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple” (Luk 14:33). The cost to be counted is total, which is precisely why it must be counted beforehand and once.
roots_summary: Welsh cwm hir, long valley; Greek purgos (G4444), a tower; Greek dapane (G1160), cost or expense; Greek ekteleo (G1615), to finish out; Greek apotassomai (G657), to renounce or forsake.
roots_lines: Welsh cwm + hir — the long valley.
Greek purgos (G4444) — a tower; “intending to build a tower” (Luk 14:28).
Greek dapane (G1160) — expense, cost; “counteth the cost” (Luk 14:28).
Greek ekteleo (G1615) — to complete, to finish out; “and was not able to finish” (Luk 14:30).
Greek apotassomai (G657) — to take leave of, to renounce; “forsaketh not all that he hath” (Luk 14:33).
usage: “sitteth not down first” (Luk 14:28) — the step the builders of Cwmhir skipped.
“begin to mock him” (Luk 14:29) — the town's verdict, reported without rebuke.
“he cannot be my disciple” (Luk 14:33) — what the parable was always about.

pos: n. (a small Cistercian abbey in Merionethshire, Wales, founded 1198; source of a silver-gilt chalice and paten hidden at the dissolution and found in 1890)
etymology: Welsh cymer, a confluence — the meeting of the rivers Mawddach and Wnion, where the abbey stands.
biblical_def: Cymer was founded in 1198 by Maredudd ap Cynan at the meeting of two rivers near Dolgellau, a daughter of Abbey Cwmhir. It was always poor: the church was never finished, the community never large, and at the dissolution its income was among the smallest in Wales. Yet in 1890 a labourer digging on a hillside above the valley turned up a silver-gilt chalice and paten of the highest quality, hidden there by someone from the abbey and never recovered by him. The pairing is the entry. A house too poor to finish its own church owned, and hid, a treasure; and Scripture puts those two facts together deliberately. “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2Co 4:7) is Paul's account of why the container is always unequal to the contents. And the kingdom itself is “like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field” (Mat 13:44). The man at Cymer hid his treasure in fear and lost it. The man in the parable hides his in joy and buys the ground.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines treasure as wealth accumulated, a great quantity of any thing collected for future use; and hide as to conceal, to withhold or withdraw from sight.
webster_full: TREASURE, n. Wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve. A great quantity of any thing collected for future use.
HIDE, v.t. To conceal; to withhold or withdraw from sight; to place in any state or position in which the view is intercepted from the object.
CHALICE, n. A cup or bowl; usually, a communion cup.
VESSEL, n. A cask or utensil proper for holding liquors and other things, as a tun, a pipe, a puncheon, a hogshead.
CONFLUENCE, n. The junction or running together of two or more streams of water.
scriptures: But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.
Mat 6:21
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
corruption_summary: A poor abbey at the meeting of two rivers, and a silver chalice hidden in a hillside by a man who never came back for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the treasure hidden out of fear rather than bought out of joy. Whoever carried the Cymer chalice up the hill in 1537 was saving it from the commissioners, and his motive may have been reverence; but the act is the same act as the servant who buried his lord's money in the earth, and it ended the same way, with the thing useless to everyone for three hundred years. A church that spends its courage on hiding what it has will not have it long.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the location of the heart. “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Mat 6:21) is not a warning against owning things; it is a diagnostic. The parable's buyer sells everything he has and is called joyful, which settles the question of whether the gospel is against wealth or merely against its being first.
roots_summary: Welsh cymer, a confluence; Greek thesauros (G2344), a treasure or storehouse; Greek ostrakinos (G3749), made of clay; Greek krupto (G2928), to hide; Greek agros (G68), a field.
roots_lines: Welsh cymer — a confluence, the meeting of waters.
Greek thesauros (G2344) — a treasure, a storehouse; “like unto treasure hid in a field” (Mat 13:44).
Greek ostrakinos (G3749) — earthen, made of baked clay; “this treasure in earthen vessels” (2Co 4:7).
Greek krupto (G2928) — to hide, to conceal; “when a man hath found, he hideth” (Mat 13:44).
Greek kardia (G2588) — the heart; “there will your heart be also” (Luk 12:34).
usage: “that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2Co 4:7) — why the vessel is always poor.
“and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath” (Mat 13:44) — the opposite of burying it.
“For where your treasure is” (Mat 6:21) — the hillside test.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Monmouthshire, Wales, founded 1179; custodian of the pilgrimage shrine and image of Penrhys)
etymology: Welsh llan, a church enclosure, with the local name Tarnam; the house was also called Dewma or Caerleon, from its first site.
biblical_def: Llantarnam was founded in 1179 by Hywel ab Iorwerth, lord of Caerleon, as a daughter of Strata Florida. Its chief business in the later Middle Ages was not farming but a shrine: the abbey owned and served the image of Our Lady of Penrhys on the ridge between the Rhondda valleys, the most frequented pilgrimage in south Wales, with a holy well below it and a steady income from offerings. In 1538 the image was taken to London and burnt at Chelsea on Cromwell's orders. The second commandment is not ambiguous about what was burnt: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4). Isaiah's satire is sharper, because he follows the workman through the process until the leftover wood becomes the god, and then “he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god” (Isa 44:17). The prophet's verdict on the worshipper is not contempt but pity: “a deceived heart hath turned him aside, that he cannot deliver his soul” (Isa 44:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines image as a representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; and idol as an image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
webster_full: IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; as an image wrought out of stone, wood or wax.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship; a pagan deity.
SHRINE, n. A case, box or repository in which sacred things are deposited; as the shrine of a saint.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable, in order to pay devotion to the relics of some deceased saint.
VOTIVE, a. Given by vow; devoted; as a votive offering.
scriptures: Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Exo 20:5

Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;
And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god.
He feedeth on ashes: a deceived heart hath turned him aside, that he cannot deliver his soul, nor say, Is there not a lie in my right hand?
corruption_summary: A Welsh abbey whose real income was a hilltop image, and the commandment that burnt it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the devotional economy — a house of prayer sustained by offerings made to a carved figure. The defence always offered is that the honour passes through the image to the person represented; Isaiah does not accept the distinction, and neither does the commandment, which forbids the making and the bowing in the same breath and attaches to it the words “for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God” (Exo 20:5). The economic fact is the giveaway: the offerings went to the shrine that had the image, not to the one that did not.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the second commandment protects the worshipper, not God's dignity alone. Isaiah ends his satire with a man who cannot ask the one question that would free him: “Is there not a lie in my right hand?” (Isa 44:20). The modern images are not carved, but the structure is identical wherever devotion attaches to a thing that can be owned, housed and charged for.
roots_summary: Welsh llan, a church enclosure; Hebrew pesel (H6459), a graven image; Hebrew temunah (H8544), a likeness; Hebrew qanna (H7067), jealous; Hebrew sheqer (H8267), a lie.
roots_lines: Welsh llan — a consecrated enclosure, a church site.
Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a carved or graven image; “any graven image” (Exo 20:4).
Hebrew temunah (H8544) — a likeness, a form; “or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4).
Hebrew qanna (H7067) — jealous; “for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God” (Exo 20:5).
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, a lie; “Is there not a lie in my right hand?” (Isa 44:20).
usage: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — the law the shrine broke.
“Deliver me; for thou art my god” (Isa 44:17) — said on a Welsh ridge for three centuries.
“He feedeth on ashes” (Isa 44:20) — the prophet's diagnosis, not his insult.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Cheshire, founded 1133 by Hugh Malbank; repeatedly disciplined for disorder and misrule)
etymology: Old English Cumbra, a Briton or Cumbrian, with mere, a lake — the Briton's lake.
biblical_def: Combermere was founded in 1133 by Hugh Malbank, baron of Nantwich, as a Savigniac house and Cistercian from 1147. Its later history is a record of visitations. Abbots were accused of selling the house's goods, of keeping armed retainers, of violence against neighbours and against their own monks; one was deposed, another resigned under charges, and in 1520 the general chapter found the community reduced and the property wasted. Few houses so plainly earned Ezekiel's indictment of the shepherds: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2), and the detail that follows, “but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them” (Eze 34:4). Peter puts the same duty positively and names the two motives that destroy it: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2), and he forbids the lordly manner outright, “Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3). The abbey's ruin was not the dissolution. It was long before.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines misrule as disorder, confusion, tumult from insubordination; and oversight as superintendence, watchful care, as the oversight of a church.
webster_full: MISRULE, n. Disorder; confusion; tumult from insubordination; unjust domination.
OVERSIGHT, n. Superintendence; watchful care; as the oversight of a church.
SHEPHERD, n. A man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep in the pasture. In a spiritual sense, a minister of the gospel.
LUCRE, n. Gain in money or goods; profit; usually in an ill sense, or with a sense of something base or unworthy.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting; particularly, the act of a superior or superintending officer, who visits a corporation, college or church, to examine into the manner in which it is conducted.
scriptures: Eze 34:2

Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?
Eze 34:4

The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost; but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
corruption_summary: A Cheshire house whose abbots fed themselves for two centuries, and the prophecy written against exactly that.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the office treated as an estate. The abbot of a great house held lands, courts, advowsons and a seat among the lords, and the temptation of the position was never chiefly sensual — it was proprietary. Ezekiel's shepherds are not accused of adultery but of eating the fat and clothing themselves with the wool while the flock scatters. “The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick” (Eze 34:4) is a charge of omission, which is how such men usually fall.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Peter's, and it is addressed to elders in ordinary congregations, not to abbots. “but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3) sets the only authority a minister has: he goes first. Where oversight is exercised by force, by constraint, or for gain, the office is already forfeit whatever the title says.
roots_summary: Old English Cumbra mere, the Briton's lake; Hebrew raah (H7462), to feed or tend; Hebrew chozqah (H2394), force or severity; Greek poimaino (G4165), to shepherd; Greek katakurieuo (G2634), to lord it over.
roots_lines: Old English Cumbra + mere — the Briton's lake.
Hebrew raah (H7462) — to pasture, to tend, to shepherd; “should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2).
Hebrew chozqah (H2394) — force, severity; “but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them” (Eze 34:4).
Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend as a shepherd; “Feed the flock of God which is among you” (1Pe 5:2).
Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to exercise lordship over; “Neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3).
usage: “that do feed themselves” (Eze 34:2) — the charge sheet of a visitation.
“not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2) — the motive test.
“being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3) — the only authority there is.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Staffordshire, founded 1176 by Bertram de Verdun; its chronicle claims the burial of King John's heart)
etymology: Old English personal name Croc with denu, a valley — Croc's valley.
biblical_def: Croxden was founded in 1176 by Bertram de Verdun, a daughter of Aunay in Normandy, and its church was built on the French plan with an apse and radiating chapels, unusual in England. Its chronicle, kept by the monk Thomas of Woodstock and others, is unusually detailed and records among much else the abbey's claim to hold the heart of King John, sent there after his death in 1216. Whether the claim is true matters less than the practice behind it, which was the division of a body among the houses that would pray for it, each taking a part and an endowment with it. Scripture has one thing to say about the heart, and it is not about burial. “Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life” (Pro 4:23) makes the heart the spring from which conduct flows, which is why its condition cannot be settled after death by anyone else. Our Lord traced the whole outward life to the same source: “For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies” (Mat 15:19). A king who divided his heart among abbeys had not kept it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heart as a muscular viscus, and figuratively the seat of the affections and passions, the inward or secret thoughts; and diligence as steady application in business of any kind.
webster_full: HEART, n. A muscular viscus, which is the primary organ of the blood's motion. The inner part of any thing. The seat of the affections and passions.
DILIGENCE, n. Steady application in business of any kind; constant effort to accomplish what is undertaken.
ISSUE, n. The act of passing or flowing out; a moving out of any inclosed place. Event; consequence.
CHRONICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
INTERMENT, n. The act of depositing a dead body in the earth; burial; sepulture.
scriptures: Pro 4:23
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies:
Jer 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
corruption_summary: A Staffordshire abbey that claimed a king's heart, and the one book that says what a heart is for.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the dismembered burial — body in one church, heart in another, entrails in a third, each with land attached, so that the prayers of three communities might be bought at once. It treats intercession as quantity and the dead man as a portfolio. Behind it lies the deeper error, the belief that the heart's standing before God remains negotiable after death, when Scripture everywhere fixes it before: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” (Jer 17:9).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that only God changes a heart, and he does it in this life by promise: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you” (Eze 36:26). That is the single remedy for a condition no endowment can touch, and it is offered to the living. The modern form of Croxden's error is the funeral that reassigns a man's standing by acclamation.
roots_summary: Hebrew leb (H3820), the heart; Hebrew mishmar (H4929), a guard or watch; Hebrew totsaah (H8444), an outgoing or issue; Greek kardia (G2588), the heart; Hebrew anash (H605), to be incurable.
roots_lines: Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, the inner man; “Keep thy heart with all diligence” (Pro 4:23).
Hebrew totsaah (H8444) — an outgoing, a source; “for out of it are the issues of life” (Pro 4:23).
Greek kardia (G2588) — the heart as the seat of thought and will; “For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts” (Mat 15:19).
Hebrew aqob (H6121) — deceitful, crooked; “The heart is deceitful above all things” (Jer 17:9).
Hebrew chadash (H2319) — new, fresh; “A new heart also will I give you” (Eze 36:26).
usage: “for out of it are the issues of life” (Pro 4:23) — why the heart is not a relic.
“who can know it?” (Jer 17:9) — the question a tomb cannot answer.
“and a new spirit will I put within you” (Eze 36:26) — the only transplant on offer.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey near Leek in Staffordshire, moved there in 1214 from Poulton; named from a founder's prayer that God would grant it increase)
etymology: Old French Dieu l'encres, God grant it increase, from the foundation legend in which the earl's wife answered a vision with that prayer.
biblical_def: Dieulacres was moved to a site near Leek in 1214 by Ranulf de Blundeville, earl of Chester, from the earlier house at Poulton which Welsh raiding had made untenable. The name comes from the foundation story: the earl, told in a vision to refound the abbey, reported it to his wife, who answered Deulacres — God grant it increase — and the words became the house's name. It is a good name and an exposed one, because increase is the one thing Scripture refuses to let any planter claim. “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) is Paul's correction of a congregation that had begun to rank its ministers, and the conclusion he draws is absolute: “So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase” (1Co 3:7). The abbey prospered moderately, quarrelled with the town, and was dissolved in 1538 like the rest. Its name outlived its walls and is still the better sermon, provided the stress falls where the Welsh countess put it, on the first word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines increase as augmentation, a growing larger, that which is added, produce, profit, interest; and plant as to set in the ground for propagation, to fix, to establish.
webster_full: INCREASE, n. Augmentation; a growing larger; extension. That which is added; the thing or things added. Produce, as of land; profit; interest.
PLANT, v.t. To put in the ground and cover, as seed for growth. To set in the ground for growth, as a young tree or a vegetable with roots.
WATER, v.t. To overflow with water; to wet or supply with water; as, to water land.
HUSBANDRY, n. The business of a farmer, comprehending agriculture or tillage of the ground.
PROSPER, v.i. To be successful; to succeed; as, to prosper in an undertaking.
scriptures: I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase.
For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building.
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
corruption_summary: An abbey whose very name is a prayer for increase, and the apostle who will not let any planter claim it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the quiet transfer of credit from the Giver to the labourer, which at Corinth took the form of parties named after preachers and in a monastery took the form of a house proud of its granges. Paul does not balance the claims; he abolishes them, and then states what the workers actually are: “For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building” (1Co 3:9). The labourers are together with God, and the field is his.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Psalmist's, which the Welsh countess was nearer to than most founders: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1). Said over a building site it sounds pious. Said over a ministry, a marriage or a business it is a hard doctrine, because it means the outcome was never in the builder's hands and the credit never was either.
roots_summary: Old French Dieu l'encres, God grant increase; Greek auxano (G837), to cause to grow; Greek phuteuo (G5452), to plant; Greek georgion (G1091), tilled land; Hebrew banah (H1129), to build.
roots_lines: Old French Dieu l'encres — God grant it increase; the countess's answer to a vision.
Greek auxano (G837) — to make to grow, to give increase; “but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6).
Greek phuteuo (G5452) — to plant; “I have planted, Apollos watered” (1Co 3:6).
Greek georgion (G1091) — a tilled field, husbandry; “ye are God's husbandry” (1Co 3:9).
Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build; “Except the LORD build the house” (Psa 127:1).
usage: “but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) — the sentence the abbey is named after.
“neither is he that planteth any thing” (1Co 3:7) — the part founders forget.
“they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1) — said over every foundation charter.

pos: n. (a small Cistercian abbey in Staffordshire, founded 1219 by Henry de Audley; the poorest of the order's houses in that county)
etymology: Old English hyll, a hill, with tun, an enclosure or farmstead — the farm on the hill.
biblical_def: Hulton was founded in 1219 by Henry de Audley as a daughter of Combermere, and it was small from the start and never grew. At the dissolution its clear annual value was under eighty pounds, with eight monks; it had no great church, no famous abbot and no chronicle. It is in this dictionary precisely for that. The Cistercian order is remembered through Rievaulx and Fountains, and the ordinary house — eight men, a hill farm, four centuries of the same office said in the same stalls — has no monument. Scripture measures by a different rule. “For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not” (2Co 8:12) is Paul's instruction to poor givers who were ashamed of their gift. Our Lord applied the same rule in the treasury, where the rich “did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living” (Mar 12:44). By that accounting Hulton may have outgiven Fountains every year of its existence, and no record survives that could tell us.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines want as deficiency, defect, the state of not having, and poverty, penury, indigence; and accept as to receive favorably, to receive with approbation.
webster_full: WANT, n. Deficiency; defect; the absence of that which is necessary or useful. Poverty; penury; indigence.
ACCEPT, v.t. To receive favorably; to receive with approbation or satisfaction.
ABUNDANCE, n. Great plenty; an overflowing quantity; ample sufficiency.
WILLING, a. Free to do or grant; having the mind inclined; disposed; not averse.
MITE, n. A very small particle or quantity; a coin of very small value.
scriptures: For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.
For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.
And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury:
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
corruption_summary: The poorest Cistercian house in Staffordshire, which the only accounting that matters may have ranked first.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the measurement of faithfulness by scale, which afflicts the church in every century and has never been more instrumented than now. The treasury scene is deliberately constructed against it: Christ is watching the amounts, he knows exactly what the rich put in, and he says “That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury” (Mar 12:43). The arithmetic is not sentimental; it is a different and truer sum.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's accounting runs on proportion and on faithfulness in small things: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luk 16:10). A small congregation that keeps the ordinances for four hundred years is not a lesser version of a large one. It is the normal case, and the large one is the exception.
roots_summary: Old English hyll tun, hill farm; Greek prothumia (G4288), readiness of mind; Greek euprosdektos (G2144), acceptable; Greek husteresis (G5304), want or penury; Greek pistos (G4103), faithful.
roots_lines: Old English hyll + tun — the farmstead on the hill.
Greek prothumia (G4288) — readiness, willingness of mind; “if there be first a willing mind” (2Co 8:12).
Greek euprosdektos (G2144) — well accepted, acceptable; “it is accepted according to that a man hath” (2Co 8:12).
Greek husteresis (G5304) — want, penury; “but she of her want did cast in all that she had” (Mar 12:44).
Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful, trustworthy; “He that is faithful in that which is least” (Luk 16:10).
usage: “and not according to that he hath not” (2Co 8:12) — the rule for a poor house.
“hath cast more in, than all they” (Mar 12:43) — the sum, done aloud.
“is faithful also in much” (Luk 16:10) — four centuries of the same office.

pos: n. (an abbey of Augustinian canons in Staffordshire, founded about 1146 by Richard Bacon; not a Cistercian house)
etymology: From the Roman station on the site, Old English ceaster, a walled town or fort, with an earlier element of uncertain sense — the old fort.
biblical_def: Rocester, founded about 1146 by Richard Bacon, nephew of the earl of Chester, was a house of Augustinian canons regular, not of Cistercian monks, and the distinction is worth an entry. A monk is bound to a cloister and a round of prayer; a canon regular is a clergyman living under rule who also serves churches, preaches and administers sacraments in the parishes his house owns. The Augustinian canons were therefore the medieval church's attempt at a settled, teaching, pastoral clergy under common discipline, and they drew their rule from the common life of the first church at Jerusalem, where “the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common” (Act 4:32). That is a real text and the canons were right to look at it. What it will not bear is the weight of a vow of poverty imposed as a condition of ministry, for the passage describes a voluntary sharing, and Peter says so to Ananias in the plainest terms: “Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power?” (Act 5:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines canon as a dignitary of the church, a person who possesses a prebend in a cathedral or collegiate church; and regular as governed by rule, living under a monastic rule.
webster_full: CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend or revenue allotted for the performance of divine service in a cathedral or collegiate church.
REGULAR, a. Instituted or initiated according to established forms or discipline; as a regular physician. Belonging to a monastic order.
CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a house inhabited by monks or nuns. A peristyle; a piazza.
COMMON, a. Belonging equally to more than one, or to many indefinitely; as, life and sense are common to man and beast.
PRIORY, n. A convent of which a prior is the superior; in dignity below an abbey.
scriptures: Act 4:32
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
Act 4:34
Neither was there any among them that lacked: for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold,
Act 5:4
Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
corruption_summary: An Augustinian house, not a Cistercian one, and the difference between a monk and a canon regular.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the use of Acts 4 as a template for compulsory common ownership, whether in a cloister or in the political schemes that have since borrowed the chapter. Luke records a spontaneous generosity in a specific church under specific pressure — “Neither was there any among them that lacked” (Act 4:34) is the result, not the rule — and the very next chapter establishes that the property remained the owner's to give or keep. Peter's question to Ananias ends the argument.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the qualifications for ministry are given plainly elsewhere and do not include celibacy or common property: “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach” (1Ti 3:2). The canons regular were reaching for something good — a disciplined, resident, teaching clergy — by a route the apostles did not lay down.
roots_summary: Latin canonicus, one on the list or rule; Greek kanon (G2583), a rule or measuring rod; Greek koinos (G2839), common; Greek homothumadon, with one accord; Greek episkopos (G1985), an overseer.
roots_lines: Latin canonicus — one enrolled on the canon or list of a church.
Greek kanon (G2583) — a measuring rod, a rule or standard.
Greek koinos (G2839) — common, shared; “but they had all things common” (Act 4:32).
Greek psuche (G5590) — soul, life; “were of one heart and of one soul” (Act 4:32).
Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer, a bishop; “A bishop then must be blameless” (1Ti 3:2).
usage: “neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own” (Act 4:32) — the text the canons built on.
“was it not in thine own power?” (Act 5:4) — the limit Peter sets on it.
“apt to teach” (1Ti 3:2) — the qualification that actually governs.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Kent, founded 1143 as a daughter of Clairvaux; keeper of the Rood of Grace, a mechanical crucifix exposed as a fraud in 1538)
etymology: Old English box, the box tree, with leah, a clearing — the clearing of box trees, on the Kentish downs.
biblical_def: Boxley was founded in 1143 by William of Ypres, a daughter of Clairvaux, and it held for four centuries the most profitable object in Kent: the Rood of Grace, a large crucifix whose figure moved its eyes, lips and head, and which was held to approve or refuse a pilgrim's offering. In February 1538 the king's commissioner Geoffrey Chamber took it down, found the wires and levers inside, showed the mechanism to the people of Maidstone, and then had it carried to London where John Hilsey displayed the works from the pulpit at Paul's Cross and burnt it. The prophets had described the object centuries before it was carved. “What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies” (Hab 2:18) names it exactly, and the woe that follows is the whole case: “Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it” (Hab 2:19). The Psalmist had already made the inventory: “They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not” (Psa 115:5). At Boxley the mouth did move, which only made the lie a mechanism.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rood as the cross, or an image of Christ on the cross; and imposture as deception practiced under a false or assumed character, fraud or imposition.
webster_full: ROOD, n. The cross; or an image of Christ on the cross, made of wood, stone or other material. A measure of land containing forty square rods.
IMPOSTURE, n. Deception practiced under a false or assumed character; fraud or imposition.
MACHINE, n. Any body or assemblage of bodies so connected as to produce effects of force and motion.
DUMB, a. Mute; silent; not speaking. Destitute of the power of speech; unable to utter articulate sounds.
DELUSION, n. The act of deluding; deception; a misleading of the mind. False representation; illusion; error or mistake proceeding from false views.
scriptures: Hab 2:18
What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?
Hab 2:19
Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach! Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it.
They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not:
They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them.
corruption_summary: The Rood of Grace, a crucifix worked by wires, and the prophets who had already written its exposure.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is complete and documented: a devotional object engineered to simulate the response of God to a payment, operated by men who knew how it worked, sustaining a community for four hundred years. It is the limiting case of the whole devotional economy, and it is worth stating plainly that the exposure was right and the burning was right. “that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols” (Hab 2:18) identifies the defendant as the maker, not merely the pilgrim.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Psalmist's law of assimilation: “They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them” (Psa 115:8). A man becomes what he worships, and the monks of Boxley, who spent four centuries operating a machine that pretended to be alive, are the most literal illustration the history of the English church affords. The warning is not aimed only at carved images; it is aimed at whatever a man builds to give him back the answer he wants.
roots_summary: Old English box leah, the box-tree clearing; Hebrew pesel (H6459), a graven image; Hebrew moreh sheqer, a teacher of lies; Hebrew ruach (H7307), breath; Hebrew batach (H982), to trust.
roots_lines: Old English box + leah — the clearing of box trees.
Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image; “What profiteth the graven image” (Hab 2:18).
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — a lie; “and a teacher of lies” (Hab 2:18).
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — breath, spirit; “there is no breath at all in the midst of it” (Hab 2:19).
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to rely on; “so is every one that trusteth in them” (Psa 115:8).
usage: “Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake” (Hab 2:19) — written for Boxley before Boxley.
“eyes have they, but they see not” (Psa 115:5) — except where wires were fitted.
“They that make them are like unto them” (Psa 115:8) — the law the operators fell under.
